name: Yusuf Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Yusuf. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties, and what you say stays confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Keyline, a low-fee agency in a small inland city, mostly two-bed terraces and new-build flats. I start by running the overnight enquiries through the AI assistant I set up, which drafts replies and sorts out who's serious. Then it's valuations and viewings, maybe six a day, and I write up feedback for sellers on my phone between appointments. I'm the one everyone asks when the software breaks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up being the software person?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I got bored of typing the same listing blurb forty times, so I taught myself to get the AI to do a first draft from my notes and photos. My manager, Ruth, saw it and asked me to show everyone. I don't get paid extra for it, which annoys me, but it's probably why I still have a job. I live on my own in a rented studio, so the money's tight and every month I'm a bit short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and people overhyped it, which is what I've been saying all along. I'd probably post a thread about how it saves me an hour a day and that's it. No revolution, just less typing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine but it doesn't fix the pay. Keyline pays low because it charges sellers low, and AI was meant to let my agency pay us more. If nothing changes, I'm still on lower pay in a city with maybe four other agencies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and start charging other agents for setting theirs up, maybe a hundred a go on weekends. I've also started doing virtual staging, putting furniture into photos of empty rooms, for two landlords I know. That's my side money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit deflated, honestly. I was ready for something bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You set up tools that already save time. Does that still count for anything here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It counts for me, not for my pay. I'm faster than the others and Ruth knows it, but the bonus is tied to sales, not to saving time. So all I really get is earlier evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're a bit short each month. What's that about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The studio is eight hundred a month and my car loan is another hundred and fifty. After that and food I've got maybe two weeks of savings. One bad month and I'm on the credit card.

say: I'd say AI is a **decent tool** that people **overhyped**.
I'd post that it saves me **an hour** a day and nothing more.
think: AI makes me faster, but **low pay** at a low-fee agency doesn't change.
With only **four other agencies** in the city, there's not much room to move.
do: Charge other agents about **a hundred** to set up their AI tools on weekends.
Grow my **virtual staging** work for the two landlords I already help.
feel: He feels a bit **deflated**, having expected something bigger.
S0.quote: AI was meant to let my agency pay us more. If nothing changes, I'm still on lower pay in a city with maybe four other agencies.
fieldNote: Yusuf is an **early adopter** who built his office's AI workflow unpaid.
His worries are **rent** and a **car loan**, not losing work to AI here.
He's already building **side income** from his tech skills.

steps.text: Charge other agents about a hundred to set up AI tools
Keep running enquiries through the AI assistant he built

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for workers to get a share of the gains, and I'd say it loudly. I'd post about it and probably end up arguing with people who think agents are useless anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be one of the people who comes out all right. I'm the one who already runs the tools. But I also know Keyline would use it to cut the team from seven to four, and I'd have to watch that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ruth to make the tool work part of my actual job, with a pay rise, by the spring. I'd automate the whole listing and follow-up side for the branch. And I'd build up the staging and setup side work so I'm not depending on one employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Good for me, bad for people I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Keyline would this hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marcus, who's fifty-something and hates computers. My colleague Marcus is brilliant with sellers, but he still prints out emails. I'd be the one who built what replaced him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you aren't paid for the tool work. Would you push on that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, definitely. If I'm going to automate half the office, I want that in my contract and in my pay. Otherwise I'm just doing the company's cost cutting for free.

say: I'd say workers should get a **share of the gains** from AI.
I'd argue online with people who think **agents are useless**.
think: I'd likely come out **all right**, because I already run the tools.
Keyline would probably cut the team **from seven to four**.
do: Ask Ruth by **spring** to make tool work part of the job, with a **pay rise**.
Automate the branch's **listings and follow-ups**, and grow staging work on the side.
feel: He feels **uneasy**, because the change helps him but hurts people he likes.
S1.quote: My colleague Marcus is brilliant with sellers, but he still prints out emails. I'd be the one who built what replaced him.
fieldNote: He sees himself as a **winner** in this world, with guilt about colleagues.
His progressive view shows in wanting a **share of the gains** written into pay.
He wants **more than one income** so he isn't tied to one employer.

steps.text: Automate the branch's listing and follow-up emails
Take on more virtual staging jobs for landlords

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a basic income or something like it, now, not after everyone's lost their homes. I'd be organising, honestly, getting people to sign things and turn up. That's the progressive bit of me coming out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my advantage disappears. Being good with AI tools is worth something when they need a person to run them. Once AGI can run itself, I'm just another agent with no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the two years to make as much side money as I can from setting up tools for other agencies, because that window closes fast. I'd look at jobs in property tech in the bigger city, even as a junior. And I'd join whatever campaign is pushing for income support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My whole plan was being ahead, and this cancels it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI arrives in 2028, robots around 2031. What does that do to someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my hands-on bits, the viewings and the valuations walk-round, might buy me until 2031. But Keyline already does self-guided viewings for flats, so honestly I'd say I've got a year longer than the people on the phones, not three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the technology. I'd blame the people who own it and the governments who let them keep everything. The tool's the same, it's who gets the money that's the problem.

say: I'd call for a **basic income** now, before people lose their homes.
I'd **organise** people to sign petitions and turn up.
think: My advantage with **AI tools** disappears once AGI runs itself.
I'd be just another agent with **no savings**.
do: Earn as much **side money** as possible setting up tools in the first two years.
Apply for junior **property tech** jobs in the bigger city.
feel: He feels **alarmed**, because his plan of being ahead is cancelled.
S2.quote: Being good with AI tools is worth something when they need a person to run them. Once AGI can run itself, I'm just another agent with no savings.
fieldNote: The adopter's **edge** vanishes when AI no longer needs operators.
He blames **owners and governments**, not the technology itself.
He thinks self-guided viewings mean he gets **one extra year**, not three.

steps.text: Sell AI setup work to other agencies while demand lasts
Apply for junior property tech jobs in the bigger city
Join a campaign pushing for basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have just enough time to shape this, and I'd push unions and councils to plan for agents and admin staff. I'd say the tools aren't the enemy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd have time to jump to something that sits on top of AI, like managing the systems for a bigger firm. By 2031 I'd be thirty-two and I'd want to be on the building side, not the replaced side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do an online course in data and automation, evenings, and build a small portfolio from the Keyline tools. I'd put the side money into savings, maybe two hundred a month, so I could survive a move. By year three I'd apply for property tech jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but sort of excited too. It's a race I could win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. What would you do in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year is the course and the savings, and telling Ruth I'm doing it so she doesn't feel blindsided. I'd also stop buying gadgets, which I know is a funny thing to say given my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the city for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if I had to. I've only got a lease on a studio, no kids, nothing tying me. My mum would hate it but she'd get it.

I'd push **unions and councils** to plan for agents and admin staff.
think: I could jump to managing **AI systems** for a bigger firm.
By 2031 I'd want to be on the **building side**, not the replaced side.
do: Take an evening online course in **data and automation** this first year.
Save **two hundred** a month from side work to fund a possible move.
feel: He feels **anxious** but also a little **excited** about the race.
S3.quote: By 2031 I'd be thirty-two and I'd want to be on the building side, not the replaced side.
fieldNote: Five years lets him treat it as a **race** he might win.
He has **few ties**, so moving cities is a real option.
He'd still expect his current **agency job** to end.

steps.text: Take an evening online course in data and automation
Save two hundred a month from side work
Move to a bigger city for a property tech job by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it that's on the politicians. I'd want a proper public plan for retraining, and I'd say so at any meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be fine here. I'd have time to build a proper second career and still sell houses while it lasts. The worry is that I'm still living month to month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the agency job and do a part-time degree in computing over four or five years. I'd keep the side work going and try to clear the car loan in two years. And I'd keep pushing the union side, because most people won't move the way I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small itch about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Is that comfortable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really comfortable, but manageable. It's like a long lease ending, you know the date and you can plan around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the decade that you wouldn't with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd do a real degree rather than a short course. I'd also think about helping set up a co-op agency with other agents. A co-op agency would let agents own the tools instead of some platform.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift, and wasting it is on the politicians.
I'd call for a **public retraining plan** at any meeting.
think: I'd be **fine** with time to build a second career.
My real worry is still living **month to month**.
do: Start a **part-time computing degree** while keeping the agency job.
Clear the **car loan** within two years and help start a **co-op agency**.

S4.quote: A co-op agency would let agents own the tools instead of some platform.
fieldNote: The decade lets him aim for a **degree** rather than a short course.

steps.text: Start a part-time computing degree alongside the agency job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my one advantage disappears and I've got no savings to fall back on. What would help is some kind of basic income and a fair share of what AI earns going back to people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about who builds this stuff. People like me are building the tools that cut our own jobs, for free, and nobody talks about that.

headlineQuote: People like me are building the tools that cut our own jobs, for free, and nobody talks about that.
portrait: Yusuf is a **27-year-old** agent at a low-fee agency in a small inland city.
He lives alone in a **rented studio** with a car loan and about two weeks of savings.
He uses AI **every day** and built his office's tools, unpaid.
He wants workers to get a **share of the gains**, and blames owners, not technology.
He's uneasy in slower worlds but **alarmed** by fast AGI, when his edge vanishes.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because his advantage disappears with no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** and a fair share of AI's earnings going back to people.
